retrieved.text: Friction opposes the motion of a block sliding down an incline. The normal force acts perpendicular to the surface and has magnitude mg cos(theta).

package.objective: Explain friction direction and normal force for a block sliding down an incline, then apply both to a new ramp angle.

components.text: For a block sliding down an incline, friction opposes the sliding motion and therefore acts up along the incline. The normal force acts perpendicular to the surface and has magnitude mg cos(theta).

components.prompt: A crate slides down a ramp toward the lower end. If the ramp angle is alpha instead of theta, what direction does friction act relative to the ramp, and what is the normal-force magnitude?
components.answer: Friction acts up the incline, opposite the crate's sliding motion. The normal-force magnitude is mg cos(alpha).

components.text: For a block on an incline, draw gravity vertically downward, the normal force perpendicular to the surface and away from it, and friction parallel to the surface opposite the sliding direction. For a ramp rising to the right with the block sliding down-left, friction points up-right along the ramp.

components.title: Forces on a block sliding down a 30° incline with μk = 0.20

components.prompt: A crate slides down a ramp that rises to the left. In axes where +x is right and +y is up, state the direction of each force: gravity, normal, and friction.
components.answer: Gravity is straight down, (0,-9.8). The normal is perpendicular to the ramp and away from it, so it points up-right. Friction is parallel to the ramp and opposes the downward slide, so it points up-left along the ramp.

generations.prompt: Build a package about torque with a diagram, an explanation, a question, a summary, and a short interactive exercise.

retrieved.text: Torque is the product of the lever arm and the applied force perpendicular to it. A beam in equilibrium has balanced clockwise and anticlockwise torques.

package.objective: Build a multi-component torque package with a beam diagram, explanation, application question, summary, and short graph-reading exercise.

components.title: Balanced beam with equal opposing torques

components.text: Torque is the turning effect of a force and equals the lever arm multiplied by the force component perpendicular to it. For a beam in equilibrium, the clockwise and anticlockwise torques balance in magnitude, so there is no net turning effect.

components.prompt: A horizontal beam is balanced about a pivot. A 6 N downward force acts 0.5 m to the left of the pivot. Where should an 8 N downward force act on the right to keep the beam level?
components.answer: 0.375 m to the right of the pivot, because the left-side torque of 6 × 0.5 = 3 N·m is matched by 8 × 0.375 = 3 N·m.

sections.heading: Torque
sections.body: Torque is the turning effect found from the lever arm and the force perpendicular to it. A force applied farther from the pivot has a larger lever arm and produces more torque for the same force.

sections.heading: Equilibrium
sections.body: A beam is in rotational equilibrium when clockwise and anticlockwise torques balance. To solve balance problems, compute each side's torque and set the opposing totals equal.

components.prompt: For the balanced beam with a 6 N force 0.5 m left of the pivot and an 8 N force on the right, the graph shows the needed right-side distance as the left-side torque changes. Read the distance when the left-side torque is 3 N·m.

components.text: On a distance-time graph, the slope of the line tells you the speed. A steeper line means a greater speed, so comparing slopes tells you which motion is faster.

components.prompt: Using the new distance-time graph above, with distance in meters and time in seconds, what speed does the line show?
components.answer: 5 m/s; the line rises 20 m over 4 s, so its slope is 5 m/s.

retrieved.text: pH is defined as the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = -log10[H+]. A solution with [H+] = 1e-3 has pH 3.

package.objective: Explain pH and apply pH = -log10[H+] to calculate pH from a hydrogen ion concentration.

components.text: pH is the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = -log10[H+]. This means each tenfold increase in [H+] lowers pH by 1 unit, so pH provides a compact scale for reporting hydrogen ion concentration.

components.prompt: A solution has [H+] = 2.5 × 10^-5 M. Calculate its pH to two decimal places.
